chapters.title: Musical notation as a Western phenomenon
Music without notation: the adhan and improvised jazz
How notation shapes Western concerts and listening
Note values, rests and dotted notes
Beat, meter, time signatures and rhythm
Hearing duple vs triple meter: Bulldog and conducting patterns
Four ways composers signal the downbeat
Ravel's Bolero: the brain finds the beat

key_points: Musical notation is mainly a Western phenomenon, used principally for art music; most of the world's music isn't notated.
Notation lets composers specify details precisely, which makes the composer more important, and it preserves works so they can be revived as intended.
With notation, the performer becomes like a carpenter following the composer-architect's blueprint, unlike pop, jazz and rock, which are made orally.
Much of the beauty of music like the Islamic call to prayer lies between the notes, which Western notation cannot capture.
Jazz musicians improvise long solos from general plans (key, chord progression, length) rather than notated or memorized music.
Notation shapes behavior: classical audiences sit silently judging accurate reproduction, while gamelan, sitar and jazz audiences interact; the eye and mind replace the ear and body.
Note values (whole, half, quarter, eighth) represent duration with duple subdivisions, rests represent silence, and a dot adds half a note's value to create triple relationships.
The beat is a steady pulse roughly at the speed of the human pulse (about 72 per minute), and meter organizes beats into groups of two or three.
In a time signature, the bottom number shows the beat unit (4 means a quarter note) and the top shows how many beats are in each measure.
Rhythm is a pattern of longs and shorts superimposed on the beat and meter.
The course covers only simple meters: students must tell duple (strong-weak) from triple (strong-weak-weak) meter and recognize basic rhythms.
Cole Porter's Bulldog is in duple meter and uses syncopation; conducting patterns (down-up, down-over-up) help listeners feel the meter.
The downbeat, the first beat of each bar, must coincide with the conductor's down motion; music may begin with a pickup before the first downbeat.
Composers signal the downbeat in four ways: longer notes, accents, low notes in the accompaniment, and chord changes, which may be the most powerful.
In Ravel's Bolero no instrument plays the beat itself; the brain extracts the beat from the combined patterns.
